note.title: School activities
note.overview: This lesson contains 50 enabled questions. It teaches School activities through explicit translation, recall, grammar and application tasks.
learningGoals: Recall the core language for School activities.
Identify the task direction before writing.
Explain errors by naming the article, subject, tense, auxiliary, agreement or negative rule.
Use the material in a short controlled sentence.
mustMemoriseRules: On means we but takes il/elle grammar.
Present uses one finite verb; perfect uses auxiliary + participle.
Use time clues to select present or past.
Rewrite the whole phrase when changing tense.

workedExamples.prompt: Change this taught form to the perfect tense: on a trop de devoirs
workedExamples.answer: on a eu trop de devoirs
workedExamples.why: Source pair: on a trop de devoirs → on a eu trop de devoirs (we have / had too much homework). Keep the auxiliary and past participle together.

workedExamples.prompt: Change this taught form to the perfect tense: on a des discussions intéressantes
workedExamples.answer: on a eu des discussions intéressantes
workedExamples.why: Source pair: on a des discussions intéressantes → on a eu des discussions intéressantes (we have / had interesting discussions). Keep the auxiliary and past participle together.

workedExamples.prompt: Change this taught form to the perfect tense: on travaille dur
workedExamples.why: Source pair: on travaille dur → on a travaillé dur (we work / worked hard). Keep the auxiliary and past participle together.

workedExamples.prompt: Change this taught form to the perfect tense: on fait des expériences
workedExamples.why: Source pair: on fait des expériences → on a fait des expériences (we do / did experiments). Keep the auxiliary and past participle together.

workedExamples.prompt: Change this taught form to the perfect tense: on s’amuse
workedExamples.why: Source pair: on s’amuse → on s’est amusé (we have / had fun). Keep the auxiliary and past participle together.

commonMistakes: Using an infinitive after on a.
A small article or ending can change the grammar even when the main vocabulary is recognisable.
Do not write on + a nous ending.
Do not use a nous ending after on.
